stem: The psychiatrist is asking a patient questions describing symptoms of mania. The patient responds, "that sounds exactly like my cousin," and proceeds to tell a long story about the cousin impulsively traveling to Mexico and exhausting all savings, never actually answering the psychiatrist's request. This is an example of:
explanation_text:
Thought process: tangential vs. circumstantial Circumstantial = takes the scenic route but ARRIVES at the point (overinclusive detail, eventually answers).
Tangential = wanders off on a tangent and NEVER returns (here: rambles about the cousin, never answers the question).
Flight of ideas = rapid jumps between loosely linked topics with pressured speech — think mania.
Clang associations = words linked by sound, not meaning (“rhyme time”).

Memory hook: Circumstantial circles back; Tangential takes off and is gone.

stem: A 70-year-old patient develops confusion, lethargy, and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Laboratory testing reveals a serum sodium of 95 mEq/l. Which of the following is the most likely complication of excessively rapid correction of this metabolic problem?
explanation_text:
Hyponatremia: correct slowly or risk ODS Serum Na of 95 is dangerously low. Correcting it too FAST causes osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis) — the pons is damaged days later.
Rule of thumb: raise Na no more than ~8 mEq/L in 24 hours.
Memory hook: “From low to high, the pons will die; from high to low, the brain will blow.” (Overcorrecting low sodium injures the pons; dropping high sodium too fast causes cerebral edema.)

stem: Which of the following SSRIs has the greatest potential for discontinuation syndrome with missed doses?

explanation_text:
Suicide prevention: restrict lethal means The strongest evidence is for reducing ACCESS to lethal means — firearm locks, blister-packing pills, barriers on bridges.

explanation_text:

Exam tip: match the described conflict to the life stage — here, forming intimate commitments.

Why hold benzodiazepines before ECT ECT works by inducing a brief, therapeutic generalized seizure. Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) RAISE the seizure threshold and shorten seizures, making ECT less effective.
So benzos are held or minimized before treatment; other anticonvulsants are reduced when possible.
If a patient truly needs a benzo, flumazenil can briefly reverse it before a session.

options.text: Episodes are commonly associated with daytime naps
Polysomnography is notable for REM sleep without atonia
Episodes occur within the first 60 minutes after sleep onset
Upon waking from an episode, these individuals are usually confused and disoriented

answer_text: Polysomnography is notable for REM sleep without atonia
answer_raw: C. Polysomnography is notable for REM sleep without atonia
explanation_text:
REM sleep behavior disorder: acting out dreams Normally REM sleep includes muscle atonia — you are temporarily paralyzed so you cannot act out dreams. In RBD that atonia is LOST, so patients physically act out vivid dreams (punching, kicking, leaping from bed).
Diagnostic finding: polysomnography shows REM sleep WITHOUT atonia.
Key association: RBD is an early warning sign of synucleinopathies — Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia. Most patients are older men.

stem: A 55-year-old patient complains of "the worst headache of my life" and is evaluated for subarachnoid hemorrhage. options.text: Outpatient follow up in one week
Repeat CT scan of the brain in 24 hours
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain

explanation_text:
Thunderclap headache: CT, then LP “Worst headache of my life” = subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise. A non-contrast CT catches most bleeds early, but its sensitivity DROPS after several hours as blood breaks down.
If the CT is negative but suspicion remains, do a lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia (yellow CSF from broken-down blood) or persistent red cells.
Bottom line: a normal CT alone does not rule out SAH.

stem: A 65-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department with memory problems and confusion over the past two days. The patient is unable to follow simple commands and disoriented on examination with no apparent focal motor deficits. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain demonstrates increased signal in the bilateral medial temporal and orbitofrontal regions and electroencephalogram (EEG) shows periodic discharges over the left temporal lobe. explanation_text:
Herpes encephalitis loves the temporal lobe Acute confusion + fever + MRI changes in the MEDIAL TEMPORAL and orbitofrontal regions + temporal periodic discharges on EEG = herpes simplex encephalitis.
It is the most common sporadic fatal encephalitis — start IV acyclovir IMMEDIATELY, even before confirmation, because delay causes death and permanent memory loss.
Do not wait for the PCR result to begin treatment.

It is strongly linked to severe, repeated early-childhood trauma.
Distinguish from dissociative amnesia (memory loss only) and depersonalization/derealization (detachment without distinct identity states).

stem: A 63-year-old patient with a history of excess alcohol intake presents with confusion. The patient is unaware of surroundings and answers only some questions with brief responses. On examination the patient is unable to move eyes laterally on either side and has nystagmus when attempting lateral gaze. The patient is unable to stand without assistance. Give IV thiamine BEFORE glucose — a glucose load without thiamine can trigger or worsen Wernicke.
Untreated it progresses to Korsakoff: irreversible memory loss with confabulation.
Mnemonic: the COA triad — Confusion, Ophthalmoplegia, Ataxia.

explanation_text:
Split brain: why the left hand can’t name things The left hemisphere holds language. The LEFT hand sends sensory information to the RIGHT hemisphere. Normally that info crosses the corpus callosum to the left (language) side to be named.
If the corpus callosum is cut or lesioned, the right hemisphere feels the object but cannot “tell” the language side — so the patient cannot name what is in the left hand, yet names right-hand objects fine.
Classic disconnection syndrome.

stem: Which of the following is the infectious neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by psychosis and abnormal gait, that was once treated with malaria-induced fever and accounted for up to 20% of patients in mental asylums until the 1940s?
explanation_text:
Neurosyphilis: the ‘great imitator’ The infectious disorder causing psychosis plus an abnormal gait — once filling asylums — is neurosyphilis (“general paresis of the insane”).
Untreated syphilis can invade the brain years later: personality change, psychosis, dementia, and tabes dorsalis (sensory ataxia), with Argyll Robertson pupils (accommodate but do not react to light).
It is still a treatable, must-not-miss cause of psychiatric symptoms — treat with penicillin.
History: the malaria cure & a Nobel Prize Before antibiotics, neurosyphilis was a death sentence and a huge share of asylum patients. In 1917 Julius Wagner-Jauregg deliberately INFECTED patients with malaria — the high fevers killed the heat-sensitive syphilis bacterium, and quinine then treated the malaria.
This “fever therapy” (pyrotherapy) was the first effective treatment for a psychiatric illness and won the 1927 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
Penicillin (1940s) made it obsolete — and asylum populations fell sharply.

Transference vs. countertransference Countertransference is the THERAPIST’s emotional reaction to the patient, shaped by the therapist’s own past relationships.
Transference is the reverse: the PATIENT projects feelings about important past figures onto the therapist.
Used well, noticing countertransference is a clinical tool — your gut reaction can reveal what the patient evokes in others.

stem: A 68-year-old patient with a history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia is evaluated in the emergency department for confusion. Prior to the onset of the episode the patient was cleaning the garage when his wife noted that he repeated himself and frequently asked, "Is everything OK?" The patient continued to clean the garage and the wife has realized that the patient did not have any recall of any activities during this time. Neurological examination was unremarkable. By that evening, the patient returned to normal with little recollection of the event. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain was normal. Which of the following is typical for this episode?

options.text: Duration of only a few hours
Associated with ischemic lesion on brain imaging

answer_text: Duration of only a few hours
answer_raw: A. Duration of only a few hours
explanation_text:
Transient global amnesia Sudden, isolated inability to form new memories (anterograde) lasting only a few hours, with repetitive questioning but preserved identity and a normal neuro exam = transient global amnesia.
It resolves on its own and rarely recurs; it is not a stroke or seizure.
Key features: abrupt, brief, memory-only, and benign.

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents with left facial droop. The emergency department physician suspects a stroke and initiates a protocol for administration of tissue plasminogen activator (TPA). Which of the following findings on neurological examination would indicate that the facial droop is not due to a stroke and therefore should not be treated with TPA?

options.text: Involvement of upper and lower face
Loss of sensation in the same distribution

answer_text: Involvement of upper and lower face
answer_raw: D. Involvement of upper and lower face
explanation_text:
Facial droop: the forehead tells the story If a facial palsy involves the WHOLE half of the face — including the FOREHEAD (cannot raise the eyebrow or close the eye) — it is a peripheral CN VII (Bell) palsy.
A central (stroke) lesion SPARES the forehead, because the upper face receives input from BOTH hemispheres.
Hook: forehead spared = central/stroke; forehead involved = peripheral/Bell.

stem: A 27-year-old patient sees a psychiatrist for what the patient describes as "panic attacks." The patient reports frequent episodes of intense fear, diaphoresis, and a sense of impending doom when in public. The episodes began two years ago, resolve spontaneously after a few minutes, and are associated with anxiety about being away from home. The patient lives with the patient's mother, who has terminal lung cancer and is on hospice care, and the patient fears that the mother will die if the patient's return home is delayed. The patient has always relied heavily on the mother and has frequent nightmares about not being able to find her. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Separation anxiety isn’t just for kids Excessive fear of being apart from a major attachment figure — here, panic tied to a dying mother — is separation anxiety disorder, now recognized in adults too.
Look for distress at separation, fear of harm befalling the loved one, and physical symptoms when apart.
It differs from panic disorder, where attacks are unexpected and not cued by separation.

A 17-year-old male patient who has been in outpatient therapy for 3 months reports having a long-standing fascination with fire that has led him to set increasingly elaborate fires. The patient describes feeling excited before setting these fires and a sense of relief afterwards. This has led him to frequently break curfew and, on several occasions, to steal the materials he needs to set the fires from a hardware store. Which of the following is the best diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Pyromania: fire for the thrill Deliberate, repeated fire-setting driven by fascination and a build-up of tension, with pleasure or RELIEF when setting or watching fires — and NOT for money, revenge, or ideology — is pyromania.
It is an impulse-control disorder; the motive is the key, since the fire itself is the reward.
Rare — rule out conduct disorder and arson for profit.

Which of the following was reported in the findings of the NIMH-funded Sequenced Treatment Alternatives to Relieve Depression (STAR*D) study?

options.text: The primary outcome of the study was response rate to SSRIs.
Every subject in the study took the same maximum dose of medication.
Fewer than one-third of subjects remitted when treated with the first SSRI.
Subjects treated by psychiatric providers became well more quickly than those treated by primary care providers.

answer_text: Fewer than one-third of subjects remitted when treated with the first SSRI
answer_raw: C. Fewer than one-third of subjects remitted when treated with the first SSRI.
explanation_text:
STAR*D: depression is hard to treat The landmark STAR*D trial found that FEWER THAN ONE-THIRD of patients remitted on their FIRST SSRI.
Remission rates fell with each subsequent step, but cumulative remission improved as treatments were switched or augmented.
Take-home: partial or non-response is common and expected — persistence, switching, and augmentation all matter.

DLPFC dysfunction is implicated in the cognitive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia (“hypofrontality”).
Think of it as the brain’s mental whiteboard.
